name: Merton Worcester

origin.place: John Innes Horticultural Institution, Merton, Surrey (now London), England
origin.parentage: Cox's Orange Pippin x Worcester Pearmain
origin.raised_by: M. B. Crane, John Innes Institute

history: Crossed at the John Innes Institute at Merton in 1914, it was not named until 1947 and reached growers around 1948; the RHS gave it an Award of Merit in 1950. The hope was a Worcester with Cox's aroma, but it turned out much more like its Worcester parent. It is a parent of the scab-resistant Gavin.

look.description: Broadly conical, greenish-yellow apple mostly covered in red, hard to tell apart from Worcester Pearmain.

taste.summary: Firm, fine-grained and juicy, with a pleasant sweet flavour. Growers describe it as an improved Worcester rather than a Cox, lacking the aromatic depth that was hoped for.

tree.notes: Reported as a regular cropper; was grown on a small commercial scale in England. Little else is recorded about the tree.

pollination.notes: The National Fruit Collection records full bloom around 10 May, a few days ahead of Cox, so group 3 is inferred. Orange Pippin rates it an average pollinator.

climate.best_climates: Cool maritime summers like southern and central England, where Worcester types colour well and keep their freshness.
climate.poor_climates: Hot summers are likely to soften the fruit and dull its colour; mild-winter regions will not meet an English apple's chill requirement.

health.other: No specific disease record found; parent Worcester Pearmain is known for some scab tolerance but mildew susceptibility.

grow_notes: Grow it as you would Worcester Pearmain: an open sunny site and a mid-season diploid partner. Pick in early September and eat within a few weeks.

name: Minnehaha

origin.place: University of Minnesota Fruit Breeding Farm, Excelsior, Minnesota
origin.parentage: Originally recorded as a Malinda seedling; a 2022 DNA pedigree study (Luby et al., cited by Wikipedia) indicates Wealthy x (Ben Davis x Fameuse).

history: The first apple released by the University of Minnesota breeding programme, selected in 1914 and introduced in 1920. Its recorded pedigree was revised by DNA work a century later.

look.description: Flattish yellow apple streaked with dark red.

taste.summary: Rather soft, coarse flesh with a mildly acid, faintly sweet flavour, according to the National Fruit Collection; little else is recorded about its eating quality.

tree.notes: Little documented beyond its Minnesota origin; bred for winter hardiness.

pollination.notes: The National Fruit Collection records full bloom around 9 May, so group 3 is inferred (group 2 is possible). Self-fertility not recorded; assume a partner is needed.

climate.best_climates: Cold continental climates with short warm summers, such as Minnesota and the upper Midwest, for which it was bred.
climate.poor_climates: Hot, humid summers are likely to give soft, poorly coloured fruit; mild-winter regions will not satisfy its chilling need.

grow_notes: Of mainly historical interest as the first Minnesota-bred apple. Treat as a hardy mid-season dessert apple and provide a pollination partner.

name: Monroe

origin.place: New York State Agricultural Experiment Station, Geneva, New York
origin.raised_by: Richard Wellington, New York State Agricultural Experiment Station

history: Crossed in 1910 at the Geneva experiment station in New York and released in the late 1940s (1947 or 1949 depending on source). It is a parent of the dark red Burgundy.

look.description: Medium, broadly conical red apple, streaked over a greenish-yellow ground; somewhat ribbed.

taste.summary: Fine-textured, rather soft cream flesh with a sweet, mildly acid flavour. Recorded as both a dessert and a cooking apple.

pollination.notes: The National Fruit Collection records full bloom around 11 May, so group 3 is inferred. Self-fertility not recorded; plant a partner.

climate.best_climates: Temperate continental climates like upstate New York, where both its parents are long established.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented; very mild winters are unlikely to meet its chilling need.

health.other: No disease information found; both parents (Jonathan, Rome Beauty) are mildew- and fire-blight-prone, but this is not confirmed for Monroe.

grow_notes: A late-season, keeping apple from New York. Pick in October and store until winter; give it a mid-season pollinator.

name: Nova Easygro

origin.place: Agriculture Canada Research Station, Kentville, Nova Scotia
origin.raised_by: A. D. Crowe, Agriculture Canada, Kentville

history: Crossed in 1956 at Kentville, Nova Scotia, and released in 1971 as a scab-resistant apple that could be grown with little spraying. It later became a parent of Novaspy.

look.description: Large, flattened apple with red stripes and blush over most of a greenish-yellow skin.

taste.summary: Firm, crisp, very white flesh with a gently sweet, mildly acid flavour and moderate juice. It is a little tough when first picked and mellows in store.
taste.best_eaten: Oct-Dec, after a few weeks in store

tree.notes: Bred for low-spray growing; little published on growth habit.

pollination.notes: Flowering group not found; assume a partner flowering mid-season is needed.

climate.best_climates: Cool, humid, scab-prone regions such as the Maritime provinces, New England and similar organic or low-spray gardens.
climate.poor_climates: Hot summers are likely to reduce colour and texture; not suited to mild-winter regions.

health.other: Bred for scab resistance (PRI source); other disease ratings not confirmed from sources read.

grow_notes: Good choice where scab is the main problem and spraying is unwanted. Store the fruit for a few weeks before eating to let it soften slightly and sweeten.

name: Novamac

origin.place: Agriculture Canada Research Station, Kentville, Nova Scotia

history: Crossed in 1963 at Kentville and introduced in 1978 as a disease-resistant McIntosh-type apple. It ripens a little before McIntosh.

look.description: McIntosh-like round-conical apple, mostly covered with dark red stripes over greenish-yellow.

taste.summary: White, fine, tender, crisp and juicy flesh with a McIntosh-style vinous flavour, sweet but with a good tart edge; slightly more wine-like than McIntosh itself.

tree.notes: Average vigour, precocious, spur-bearing and a regular cropper (Orange Pippin).

pollination.notes: Orange Pippin lists group 4. Blossom is susceptible to frost.

climate.best_climates: Cool northern climates where McIntosh does well: Atlantic Canada, New England, northern Europe.
climate.poor_climates: Hot summers give soft, poorly coloured McIntosh types; frost-prone spring sites risk the blossom.

health.other: Resistant to scab, cedar-apple rust and fire blight but susceptible to powdery mildew (Brooks & Olmo register via Wikipedia). Short keeper.

grow_notes: An easy, low-spray McIntosh substitute; watch for mildew and avoid frost pockets. Eat within a few weeks of picking.

name: Novaspy

origin.place: Agriculture Canada Research Station, Kentville, Nova Scotia
origin.parentage: Nova Easygro x (Northern Spy x Golden Delicious)

history: Released at Kentville in 1986 as a scab-resistant apple in the style of Northern Spy. Opinions differ on whether it matches Spy for flavour.

look.description: Large round apple with a variable (roughly a third to most of the skin) dark red or orange-red flush.

taste.summary: Creamy-yellow, fine, firm, crisp and juicy flesh with a mildly acid, fairly sharp flavour. Tasters are divided: some find it less tart and complex than Northern Spy, others like it, especially baked or dried.

tree.notes: Average vigour, precocious, partly tip-bearing and a good regular cropper (Orange Pippin); unlike Northern Spy it starts bearing early.

pollination.notes: Orange Pippin lists group 3, not self-fertile.

climate.best_climates: Cold-temperate and mild damp climates; hardy to about USDA zone 4.
climate.poor_climates: Hot-summer regions are likely to give poor colour; mild-winter regions lack chill.

health.other: Scab resistant; Orange Pippin rates it very resistant to fire blight.

grow_notes: A low-spray, late keeping apple for cold gardens. Being partly tip-bearing, prune lightly with renewal cuts rather than hard spur pruning.

name: Ohio Nonpareil

origin.place: Orchard of Mr Bowman, Massillon, Ohio

history: Arose in Mr Bowman's orchard at Massillon, Ohio and was described in 1848. It was an important regional apple in 19th-century Ohio and is often compared to Gravenstein.

look.description: Large, flattish, slightly ribbed apple; pale greenish-yellow with a pinkish-orange flush streaked and mottled carmine, and russet dots.

taste.summary: Firm, crisp, fairly fine yellowish flesh, juicy, with a sweet, gently acid and aromatic flavour. Often likened to Gravenstein (sweet yet savoury) but with firmer flesh.

tree.notes: Recorded as a vigorous, healthy tree.

pollination.notes: Early flowering: the National Fruit Collection records full bloom around 6 May, so group 2 is inferred. Use an early-to-mid flowering partner.

climate.best_climates: Midwestern and eastern US climates with warm summers, where it was a regional favourite.

health.other: No disease information found beyond a note that the tree is healthy.

grow_notes: An early-autumn dual-purpose apple for baking or eating fresh. It keeps only a month or two, so pick in succession and use promptly.

name: Oliver
history: An Ozark apple from north-western Arkansas, known by 1873, later sold widely under the nursery name Senator. It was valued in the region as an attractive winter keeper.

look.description: Flattish, glossy apple almost covered in crimson streaked darker red, with prominent pale or russet dots.

taste.summary: Crisp, tender, breaking, juicy flesh with a lively, mildly acid flavour that turns towards sweet as it keeps; described as rich and refreshing.

pollination.notes: Flowering group not recorded; plant a partner.

climate.best_climates: Warm-summer upland regions of the southern and central US such as the Ozarks, where it originated.
climate.poor_climates: Not documented; as a late southern apple it may not ripen fully in short, cool seasons.

grow_notes: A late-keeping Ozark heirloom. Pick late, store cool, and eat through winter; give it a pollination partner.
